item.title: 7 Habits that make you a better listener and build trust
item.description: Discover seven simple listening habits that strengthen relationships, build trust and help you become more understanding and approachable.
item.content:encoded:
Being a good listener is more than staying quiet while someone else speaks. It involves giving people your attention, understanding their perspectives and making them feel heard without immediately offering advice or judgement.

In everyday conversations, people often focus on what they want to say next rather than understanding what the other person is trying to communicate. This can lead to misunderstandings, weakened relationships and a lack of trust.

Good listening, on the other hand, makes people feel respected and comfortable expressing themselves. Whether you are communicating with friends, family members or colleagues, developing better listening habits can improve the quality of your relationships.

Here are seven habits that can help you become a better listener and build stronger connections with people.

7 Habits that make you a better listener and build trust

1. Give your undivided attention

One of the simplest ways to become a better listener is to give someone your full attention when they are speaking. Constantly checking your phone, looking around or thinking about unrelated tasks can make the other person feel unimportant.

Put away distractions, maintain natural eye contact and focus on the conversation. Even small gestures, such as nodding occasionally, can show that you are actively following what someone is saying.

When people realise they have your attention, they are more likely to feel comfortable sharing their thoughts.

2. Listen without interrupting

Interrupting someone before they finish expressing their thoughts can make them feel unheard or dismissed. Even when you have something important to add, allow the other person to complete their sentence.

Give them enough time to explain their feelings, experiences or opinions without rushing the conversation. You do not always need to respond immediately.

Sometimes, allowing someone to finish speaking is more valuable than having the perfect response ready.

3. Ask thoughtful questions

Good listeners do not simply hear words; they try to understand the meaning behind them. Asking thoughtful questions helps you understand someone's perspective and encourages a more meaningful conversation. Instead of immediately changing the subject, ask questions such as, "How did that make you feel?" or "What happened after that?"

Avoid turning the conversation into an interrogation. Your questions should come from genuine curiosity rather than an attempt to prove a point.

4. Avoid judging too quickly

People often hesitate to share their experiences because they fear being judged. Making assumptions, criticising their decisions or immediately telling them what they should have done can discourage honest communication.

Try to understand the situation from their perspective before forming an opinion. Remember that everyone has different experiences, circumstances and ways of dealing with challenges.

You do not have to agree with everything someone says to respect their feelings and listen without judgement.

5. Pay attention to body language

Communication is not limited to spoken words. Facial expressions, posture, tone of voice and gestures can reveal emotions that someone may find difficult to express directly.

For example, a person might say they are fine while their tone or expression suggests otherwise. Noticing these signals can help you understand what they might be experiencing.

Maintain an open posture, avoid looking impatient and respond naturally to their expressions. Being attentive to non-verbal communication makes conversations more thoughtful and empathetic.

6. Do not rush to give advice

When someone shares a personal problem, it is natural to want to offer solutions. However, not everyone is looking for advice. Sometimes, people simply want someone who will listen and understand what they are going through.

Before suggesting a solution, ask, "Would you like my advice, or would you prefer me to listen?"

This small question can make a significant difference. It shows that you respect their needs instead of assuming you know what is best for them.

7. Remember what people share with you

Remembering small details from previous conversations shows people that you genuinely pay attention to what they say.

It could be an important meeting they mentioned, a family event they were looking forward to or a personal goal they were working towards.

Following up with a simple question, such as "How did your interview go?" or "Did everything work out with your project?" can make someone feel valued.

It also demonstrates that your interest in their lives goes beyond a single conversation.

Final thoughts

Becoming a better listener does not require complicated communication techniques. It starts with small, consistent actions such as giving people your attention, asking thoughtful questions and allowing them to express themselves without interruption.

When people feel heard rather than judged, they are more likely to open up and build meaningful connections.

Trust is built over time through consistent actions. Sometimes, one of the most valuable things you can offer another person is your willingness to listen and understand.

item.title: 6 Must-read Indian historical fiction books to explore
item.description: Explore six must-read Indian historical fiction books that bring the past to life through stories of royal empires, colonial rule, love and Partition.
item.content:encoded:
India's history is filled with royal dynasties, political conflicts, colonial struggles, cultural transformations and stories of extraordinary people. While history books document these events, historical fiction offers another way to experience them through fictional characters and imaginative interpretations of real events.

From the Mughal courts and the final days of the Sikh Empire to the British colonial period and the Partition of 1947, Indian historical fiction explores different eras through compelling storytelling. These novels combine historical settings with themes of love, ambition, identity, courage and survival.

Here are six must-read Indian historical fiction books that offer an engaging way to explore the country's past.

6 Historical fiction books that explore India's fascinating past

1. The Glass Palace by Amitav Ghosh

Set against the backdrop of the British invasion of Burma in 1885, The Glass Palace follows the lives of several families whose stories unfold across Burma, India and Malaya.

The novel begins with Rajkumar, a young orphan who witnesses the fall of the Burmese monarchy and the exile of its royal family. As the British take control, Rajkumar builds a new life through the timber trade, while his personal journey becomes connected with the lives of people affected by colonialism, migration and war.

Spanning nearly a century, the story explores the consequences of British imperialism, economic exploitation and political upheaval. Amitav Ghosh also examines how historical events shape individual identities and relationships across generations.

2. The Twentieth Wife by Indu Sundaresan

The Twentieth Wife takes readers into the world of the Mughal Empire through the remarkable journey of Mehrunnisa, who later becomes Empress Nur Jahan.

Born into a Persian family, Mehrunnisa grows up with ambitions that extend beyond the traditional expectations placed on women. Her life takes an unexpected turn when she meets Prince Salim, the future Emperor Jahangir. Their relationship develops over several years, eventually bringing her into the centre of Mughal political and royal life.

The novel explores palace politics, royal marriages, ambition and the challenges faced by women in a male-dominated society. It also offers a glimpse into the customs, traditions and power structures of the Mughal court.

Indu Sundaresan blends historical details with fictional storytelling to imagine the life of one of the most influential women in Mughal history.

3. The Last Queen by Chitra Banerjee Divakaruni

The Last Queen centres on Maharani Jindan Kaur, who rose to prominence as the wife of Maharaja Ranjit Singh and mother of Maharaja Duleep Singh, the last ruler of the Sikh Empire.

Set during the decline of the Sikh Empire in the nineteenth century, the novel follows Jindan's transformation from a young woman into a queen who becomes deeply involved in the political struggles of her kingdom.

After Ranjit Singh's death, the empire faces internal conflicts and growing British interference. Jindan fights to protect her son's position and preserve the independence of the Sikh kingdom. However, political conspiracies and colonial ambitions gradually change the course of her life.

The novel highlights the strength, determination and sacrifices of a woman who refused to remain a silent figure in history. It also explores motherhood, power, betrayal and resistance during a significant period in Indian history.

Also Read
5 Non-fiction books you must read before 2026 ends

4. The Henna Artist by Alka Joshi

Set in post-independence Jaipur, The Henna Artist follows Lakshmi as she rebuilds her life after escaping an abusive marriage and establishes herself as an independent woman.

After arriving in Jaipur, she establishes a successful career as a henna artist, serving wealthy women from influential families. Her artistic skills and knowledge of traditional remedies make her a trusted confidante among the city's elite.

However, Lakshmi's carefully built life is disrupted when her younger sister, Radha, unexpectedly enters her world. Their reunion brings family secrets, difficult choices and emotional complications that threaten the independence Lakshmi has worked so hard to achieve.

Through its detailed portrayal of post-independence Jaipur, the novel explores class differences, women's independence, social expectations and the changing position of women in Indian society.

5. The Book of Everlasting Things by Aanchal Malhotra

Aanchal Malhotra's The Book of Everlasting Things is a historical novel set against the backdrop of the Partition of India in 1947.

The story follows Samir Vij, a young Hindu apprentice in his family's perfume business, and Firdaus Khan, a Muslim girl from Lahore. Their lives become intertwined through their shared affection and growing relationship.

As political tensions rise and the Partition divides the subcontinent, the two find themselves caught in circumstances beyond their control. The division of their homeland brings displacement, separation and uncertainty into their lives.

The novel uses the world of perfumes, memories and sensory experiences to explore how people hold on to their identities, relationships and cultural roots during periods of immense change.

It also examines the emotional consequences of migration and the lasting impact of Partition on families and future generations.

6. Train to Pakistan by Khushwant Singh

Train to Pakistan is one of the most recognised Indian novels about the Partition of 1947. Written by Khushwant Singh, it explores the human consequences of the division of India through the experiences of people living in a small Punjab village called Mano Majra. Before Partition, Mano Majra is home to both Sikh and Muslim communities who have lived together peacefully for generations. However, as the country is divided, violence and fear gradually enter the village. The arrival of trains carrying dead bodies from across the newly created border changes the atmosphere completely. The villagers are forced to confront religious tensions, political uncertainty and difficult moral choices.

At the centre of the story are Juggut Singh and Iqbal, two men whose lives become connected with the unfolding tragedy. Their experiences reveal how ordinary people are affected by decisions made during moments of political upheaval.

Rather than focusing only on political leaders and historical events, Khushwant Singh presents Partition through the lives of ordinary individuals.

Final thoughts

Historical fiction allows readers to explore the past beyond dates, battles and political events. Through personal experiences, relationships and fictional characters, these novels offer a deeper understanding of the people and societies that shaped India's history.

Whether it is the grandeur of the Mughal Empire in The Twentieth Wife, the courage of Maharani Jindan Kaur in The Last Queen or the heartbreaking realities of Partition in Train to Pakistan, each book presents a different perspective on the country's past.

For readers looking to explore Indian history through literature, these six novels are a wonderful place to begin.

item.title: 8 Carl Jung ideas that explain why you repeat mistakes
item.description: Explore eight Carl Jung ideas that explain why you repeat mistakes, repeat unhealthy patterns, and struggle to change your behaviour.
item.content:encoded:
Repeating the same mistakes can be frustrating, especially when you are aware of what went wrong the last time. You may promise yourself that things will be different, only to find yourself making similar choices in relationships, work, or everyday life.

Swiss psychiatrist and psychoanalyst Carl Jung believed that much of human behaviour is influenced by the unconscious mind. According to his theories, unresolved emotions, hidden fears, and unrecognised patterns can shape decisions without us fully realising it.

His ideas offer an interesting way to understand why people sometimes repeat behaviours they consciously want to change.

Here are eight Carl Jung ideas that can help explain why you keep repeating the same mistakes.

8 Carl Jung theories that explain why you repeat mistakes

1. The unconscious mind influences your choices

Jung believed that the unconscious mind plays a significant role in shaping human behaviour. Not every decision comes from conscious thinking. Past experiences, suppressed emotions, and hidden beliefs can influence how people react to situations.

For example, someone who experienced rejection may repeatedly choose relationships where they feel unappreciated because familiar emotional patterns influence their choices.

The lesson: Becoming aware of what drives your decisions can help you stop reacting automatically.

2. The shadow contains the parts of yourself you avoid

One of Jung's most recognised concepts is the shadow. It refers to the parts of your personality that you do not readily acknowledge or accept. These may include jealousy, insecurity, anger, fear, or even positive qualities you have learned to suppress.

When you refuse to recognise these feelings, they can influence your behaviour indirectly. For instance, someone who refuses to acknowledge their insecurity may repeatedly seek validation from others.

The lesson: Accepting uncomfortable parts of yourself is an important step towards understanding your behaviour.

3. Repressed emotions can return in different forms

Jung explored how unacknowledged psychological experiences can continue to influence a person's life. Avoiding painful emotions does not necessarily make them disappear.

For example, someone who never addresses their anger may repeatedly become defensive during minor disagreements. The reaction may appear disproportionate because it is connected to unresolved feelings.

The lesson: Instead of constantly distracting yourself from uncomfortable emotions, try to understand where they come from.

Also Read
Carl Jung’s life-changing lessons you’ll wish you knew sooner

4. Complexes can trigger repeated reactions

Jung used the term complexes to describe emotionally charged groups of thoughts, memories, and associations that can influence behaviour.

A person with strong feelings around rejection, for example, may interpret neutral feedback as criticism. This can lead to defensiveness, misunderstandings, and repeated conflicts.

These reactions may happen automatically because the situation activates an existing emotional complex.

The lesson: Notice which situations trigger unusually strong emotional reactions and explore the experiences connected to them.

5. Projection makes you overlook your own patterns

Projection is a psychological concept Jung explored to explain how people can attribute their own unrecognised feelings or qualities to others.

For instance, someone who struggles to accept their own jealousy may constantly accuse others of being jealous. This can prevent them from recognising what is happening within themselves.

When you focus entirely on other people's behaviour, you may overlook the patterns that contribute to your own difficulties.

The lesson: Before judging someone's actions, ask yourself whether your reaction reveals something you have not acknowledged about yourself.

6. Individuation requires becoming more self-aware

Individuation is one of Jung's central ideas. It describes the lifelong process of becoming a more integrated and authentic individual by recognising and bringing different aspects of the personality into awareness.

This includes understanding your strengths, weaknesses, fears, desires, and contradictions.

Without self-awareness, people may continue following expectations, repeating familiar choices, and ignoring what they genuinely need.

The lesson: Personal growth begins when you understand yourself rather than constantly trying to become someone others expect you to be.

7. Unresolved conflicts can keep you emotionally stuck

Jung believed that psychological development involves recognising and working through opposing forces within the personality.

For example, you may want independence while simultaneously fearing loneliness. This internal conflict can lead you to repeatedly make decisions that contradict your actual needs.

Until you recognise both sides of the conflict, you may struggle to understand why you keep changing your mind or returning to familiar situations.

The lesson: Acknowledge conflicting feelings instead of pretending that only one side exists.

8. What you resist can influence your behaviour

Jung's psychological work explored how resisting or avoiding aspects of ourselves can give them greater influence over our lives.

When you refuse to acknowledge a fear, insecurity, or uncomfortable truth, it may continue shaping your decisions without your awareness.

For example, someone who fears failure may repeatedly postpone important opportunities while convincing themselves that they are simply waiting for the right moment.

The lesson: Recognising what you are avoiding can help you understand the reasons behind repeated behaviours.

Final thoughts

Carl Jung's ideas offer a valuable perspective on why people sometimes repeat the same mistakes despite wanting to change. His work highlights the importance of understanding the unconscious mind, recognising emotional patterns, and accepting the parts of ourselves we often avoid.

Breaking a repeated pattern does not always begin with making a bigger effort. Sometimes, it begins with asking better questions: Why do I react this way? What am I avoiding? Which experience might be influencing this decision? The more honestly you examine your behaviour, the easier it becomes to recognise patterns and make more conscious choices. Self-awareness cannot guarantee that you will never repeat a mistake, but it can help you understand your actions and respond differently next time.

item.title: India AI funding nearly doubles to $1.6B in Jan-Sept 2026: Tracxn
item.description: Early-stage funding led the investment mix. Mumbai overtook Bengaluru to become the city with the largest funding during the period.
item.content:encoded:
India AI companies raised $1.6 billion in equity funding in the first nine months of 2026, nearly double the level in the year-ago period, according to a report by Tracxn Technologies.

This, in fact, is the highest funding grosser across the nine-month periods covered since 2019.

"India AI companies raised $1.6 billion in equity funding in nine months 2026, up 96% from $822 million in nine months 2025 and 162% from $616 million in nine months 2024, marking the highest funding total across the nine-month periods covered since 2019," the report by data intelligence platform Tracxn Technologies' said.

According to the 'India AI - 9M 2026' report, the funding was raised across 87 rounds, compared to 149 rounds during the year-ago period. This indicates that the increase was driven by a relatively small number of large deals.

Early-stage funding led the investment mix. Mumbai overtook Bengaluru to become the city with the largest funding during the period.

The ten largest rounds in 2026 raised $1.5 billion, 90% of the $1.6 billion total.

Neysa, a Mumbai-based AI cloud provider, raised the largest chunk, a $600 million Series B in February, equivalent to 37% of all funding. Sarvam, the Bengaluru-based generative AI developer, raised $255 million in a Series B in June and a further $90.4 million in August. Yotta raised $150 million in July.

"Series A and later rounds fell 33% to 24 from 36, and first-time funded companies fell 60% to 24 from 60," the report said.

Globally, AI companies raised $383.5 billion in the first nine months of 2026; India's $1.6 billion was 0.4% of that, ninth among countries.

Early-stage funding rose 191% to $1.3 billion between January and September, up from $434 million in the year-ago period. Early-stage rounds fell 38% to 21. The average early-stage round was $60.2 million against $12.8 million in the year-ago period.

According to the report, 111 investors backed India AI companies in the first nine months of 2026, down from 169 in the year-ago period. First-time investors fell to 43, and international investors fell to 29.

Peak XV Partners led early-stage investors with three investments, followed by Prosus and Khosla Ventures with two each. Antler, IvyCap Ventures and Finvolve made two seed investments each, while SoftBank Vision Fund and Creaegis backed one late-stage round each.

item.title: Maharashtra GST Department conducts search at Turtlemint subsidiary
item.description: The filing has added that the regular business operations of Turtlemint and TIB remains unaffected.
item.content:encoded:
The Maharashtra Goods and Services Tax (GST) has initiated inspection,search and seizure proceedings at the premises of Turtlemint Insurance Broking Services, according to a regulatory filing on November 24. 

The search was conducted at Turtlemint Insurance Broking Services Private Limited (“TIB”), a wholly owned subsidiary of the Company at its registered office situated at Mumbai. 

“TIB is extending full cooperation to the concerned authorities and is providing the requisite information, documents and clarifications as may be required in connection with the proceedings,” said the filing. 

Turtlemint will keep the Stock Exchanges informed of further developments, if any, in accordance with applicable laws and regulations.

The filing has added that the regular business operations of Turtlemint and TIB remains unaffected. It also said that the company and TIB “remains commiƩed to conduct its business in compliance with the applicable laws and regulations.”

Founded in 2015 by Dhirendra Mahyavanshi and Anand Prabhudesai, Turtlemint operates an insurance distribution platform. It competes with companies such as Policybazaar and InsuranceDekho in India's digital insurance segment.

item.title: Enterprise data security startup Matters.AI raises Rs 115 Cr in pre-Series A round
item.description: Matters.AI gives security teams one source of truth for sensitive data, showing where it is, where it has travelled, who or what has touched it, and whether that use was intended.
item.content:encoded:
Bengaluru-based enterprise data security startup Matters.AI has raised about Rs 115 crore ($12 million) in a pre-Series A round led by Tanglin Venture Partners.

IIFL Fintech Fund, Piper Serica’s Bharat Tech Fund, Foster Ventures, and Tetration Ventures joined the round, along with existing investors Kalaari Capital and Endiya Partners.

The round brings the startup's total funding to about Rs 175 crore ($18.25 million), Matters.AI said in a statement.

The company will use the fresh capital for research and development in data lineage, autonomous investigation, endpoint and browser intelligence, and prevention of sensitive data misuse by AI agents. It will also build its North American sales team, starting with senior leadership hires.

According to the statement, AI agents now read, copy and move enterprise data with the permission of the employees who run them. Most data security tools show where sensitive data sits. They do not show who or what is using it, or why. So security teams connect alerts from separate tools before they can respond.

Matters.AI says it gives security teams one source of truth for sensitive data, showing where it is, where it has travelled, who or what has touched it, and whether that use was intended. It builds a picture using AI to understand the context of the data and the intent behind each use.

The startup brings together elements that enterprises buy as separate products for data security posture management, insider risk, activity monitoring and data loss prevention.

Matters.AI is deployed in more than 50 organisations, including major financial institutions, stockbroking and asset management firms, large retailers, and digital media and entertainment platforms. 

“Security teams don’t need another tool telling them something might be wrong. They need a system that understands the problem, investigates it, and takes action," said Keshava Murthy, Co-founder and CEO of Matters.AI.

He added, "We built Matters.AI with a simple conviction. Enterprise data security should evolve from fragmented tools and manual investigations into an AI security engineer capable of doing the work.

"As AI agents increasingly access and move sensitive information alongside humans, we believe every enterprise will need an AI security engineer protecting its most valuable asset, its data.”

Sankalp Gupta, Managing Partner at Tanglin Venture Partners, believes enterprise data security is at an inflection point.

He said, ”As AI agents increasingly operate alongside humans, the challenge is no longer just knowing where sensitive data resides, but understanding how its being used and acting before it becomes a risk.

"Matters.AI stood out to us for its fundamentally different approach, building an AI security engineer that combines deep data intelligence, identity behaviour, and autonomous investigation and remediation. Rather than adding another layer of alerts, the team is rethinking how enterprise data security operates."

item.title: How flexibility, services, and employee experience are driving IndiQube’s growth
item.description: IndiQube, which manages close to 11 million square feet of office space, is broadening its offerings through integrated services, design solutions, and sustainability offerings to drive growth and enhance employee experience.
item.content:encoded:
Managed office space provider IndiQube continues to see strong demand as it expands its offering to cater to the growing requirements of the market.

Founded in 2015, IndiQube entered the market at a time when India's startup ecosystem was witnessing rapid growth, driven by sectors such as ecommerce, mobility, and food delivery. The founders realised that similar disruption would also come into the real estate sector, which offered limited flexibility and standardised services.

The company identified three key requirements for businesses: flexibility, services, and a superior employee experience. It has since evolved into an integrated managed workspace provider, serving 884 clients.

IndiQube reported a 34% year-on-year rise in revenue to Rs 492 crore in the second quarter of FY27, while narrowing its losses by 80% to Rs 6 crore.

At the end of the quarter, the company was present in 17 cities with 138 centres and managing 10.86 million square feet of space.

In an interview with YourStory, Meghna Agarwal, Co-founder of IndiQube, highlighted the company’s growth drivers and what are they doing to remain ahead of the game.

Edited excerpts.

YourStory (YS): How do you see IndiQube’s performance in the second quarter of FY27?

Meghna Agarwal (MA): Our profitability has improved due to our steady state of occupancy, which has increased from 89% to 91%, which has boosted our growth. Given our economies of scale, we expect our top line revenue growth to be in the range of about 30% and EBITDA to be in the range of 19-21%, and our PAT would be in the range of about 8-10%.

YS: What are the factors that are driving demand for IndiQube?

MA: Earlier, it was startups. But now we have expanded into Indian enterprises, multi-national corporations, and global capability centres (GCCs), which is a balanced mix.

In terms of the cities, it is very important to have a presence in Tier I locations because of the presence of a large number of companies. Among the top 10 cities, Bengaluru is the largest in terms of area. It is not that we just focus on top tier cities as we are also present in places such as Coimbatore and Madurai.

Our strategy is to have a wider presence as well as go deeper in the existing cities. For example, a client will be keen to have multiple locations within the city of Bengaluru or Mumbai. A deeper penetration gives us economies of scale and we keep testing the water with a wider presence. It has to be a balance between both.

YS: How is IndiQube expanding its offerings for customers?

MA: We call ourselves a managed integrated platform. I have four models. One is the growth, which is plug and play services. Second is DesignQube, which provides interior services where we do it not only for IndiQube clients but also for non-IndiQube customers. Third is IndiQare where we provide services like food, transport, etc., and there is consistency of experience regardless of their location. Lastly, it is the eco-sustainability solutions, which looks into energy and water management, green buildings, etc.

YS: What do you think are the USPs of IndiQube?

MA: Our biggest asset is the manner in which we lease properties. We are not tied to a building or asset, but to talent. Wherever the talent is going, we will go there. For example, we have renovated one-third of the properties in our portfolio. Second is the flexibility in our offerings where it can range from Rs 8,000 per seat going all the way up to Rs 20,000. Third is the wide array of services that we provide where we ensure that the quality and experience remains the same across all our properties. The fourth part, which is very underrated, is corporate governance. The intent of the founders has always been to create value for everyone—clients, shareholders, and the team. Lastly, it is our focus on sustainability and we have been doing this since early 2000. Today, around 85% of our properties are green certified buildings. IndiQube places emphasis on building long-term relationships with our clients.

item.title: Aeravti Ventures launches Rs 300 Cr fund II
item.description: The second fund of Aeravti Ventures will invest in around 10 startups in segments of food security, health infra and physical security.
item.content:encoded:
Aeravti Ventures, a Bengaluru-based early stage venture capital firm, has launched its second fund called Aeravti Ventures II, with a target corpus of Rs 300 crore.

A statement from the VC firm said, Aeravti Ventures II has secured commitments as first close of its target corpus with the final close expected within the next six months.

Aeravti Ventures II plans to invest in approximately 9–10 startups spanning pre-seed to pre-Series A stages, with a preference for leading pre-seed and seed rounds. The fund expects to write initial cheques of Rs 6–10 crore per startup with the capacity to invest 2–3 times the initial amount in subsequent funding rounds.

Fund II will focus on three investment themes: food security, health infrastructure and physical Security. These investments will span opportunities across agriculture and allied sectors, biosciences, life sciences, advanced manufacturing, waste management and energy.

The fund also marks an expansion of Aeravti’s investment focus into physical infrastructure-led businesses, a segment that is becoming increasingly important to India’s long-term growth and development.

On the launch and sector focus, Rishabh Singh, Managing Partner at Aeravti Ventures said "We believe these sectors require patient capital, a long-term outlook and investors who understand the complexities of building in them. With Fund II, we want to back founders addressing these gaps early and help build businesses that can create lasting value for the Indian economy."

The new fund builds on the track record of Aeravti’s first fund, which achieved a final close of Rs 76 crore and is fully deployed across seven companies, with the VC firm having led the seed round in each of the investments. It further added that of these seven portfolio companies, a few have raised follow-on funding, while three are currently operating profitably.

Shubham Jhuria, Partner and CFO at Aeravti Ventures said that Fund I gave them valuable experience in identifying founders early and supporting businesses through different stages of growth. “With Fund II, we are building on that foundation with a more focused investment strategy, a stronger team and the ability to support our portfolio companies through follow-on investments as they scale," he added.

item.title: Google Cloud confirms 30 role cuts in India, rejects claims of wider layoffs
item.description: However, Google Cloud has not identified the teams involved or disclosed the exit terms.
item.content:encoded:
Google Cloud has confirmed that around 30 roles in India were eliminated last week due to work reprioritisation. It, however, rejected online claims that much of its local workforce had been affected.

“These rumors are totally inaccurate. Last week, Google Cloud made a small organizational change in India, and approximately 30 roles were eliminated as part of a re-prioritization of work,” the company said in response to a user on X.

However, Google Cloud has not identified the teams involved or disclosed the exit terms. Anonymous posts on workplace forum Blind mention abrupt dismissals and short resignation deadlines, but these allegations remain unverified.

The clarification comes as Google Cloud is expanding its business rapidly. Its parent company Alphabet’s third-quarter results showed cloud revenue rising 103% year on year to $30.7 billion, driven by demand for AI infrastructure, AI services, and the wider cloud platform. 

However, strong business growth does not mean every team or role is expanding at the same pace. This discrepancy is visible across the technology sector.

In 2023, Google announced 12,000 job cuts globally. Since then it since made smaller, targeted reductions. Reuters reported that Google expanded voluntary exit offers to some employees in five countries this summer as it managed costs amid heavy AI investment. 

Microsoft offered voluntary buyouts to about 60,000 eligible employees in October this year, indicating the wider trend of 'workforce adjustment' in the industry.

India remains a major market for cloud infrastructure. Amazon Web Services broke ground on an expanded data centre in Hyderabad in July. It said it plans to invest more than $21 billion in Indian cloud and AI infrastructure between 2026 and 2030. 

Meanwhile, the Government of India issued a cloud selection framework in March, guiding ministries to choose services according to the sensitivity and criticality of their data, including hybrid-cloud options that combine public and private infrastructure.

Edited by Swetha Kannan

item.title: Startup news and updates: Daily roundup (November 24, 2026)
item.description: YourStory presents the daily news roundup from the Indian startup ecosystem and beyond. Here's the roundup for Tuesday, November 24, 2026.
item.content:encoded:
From Google Cloud cutting jobs in India to Keralam’s new initiative, 'Avalkkoppam' (With Her), to tackle domestic and cyber violence against women, here are the latest developments across sectors.

Featured Stories

Google Cloud confirms 30 role cuts in India, rejects claims of wider layoffs

Google Cloud has confirmed that around 30 roles in India were eliminated last week due to work reprioritisation. It, however, rejected online claims that much of its local workforce had been affected.

“These rumors are totally inaccurate. Last week, Google Cloud made a small organizational change in India, and approximately 30 roles were eliminated as part of a re-prioritization of work,” the company said in response to a user on X.

Read more

Latest News

Keralam to roll out 'Avalkkoppam' initiative against domestic, cyber violence targeting women

Keralam will roll out a new initiative, 'Avalkkoppam' (With Her) to tackle domestic and cyber violence against women as part of a 16-day statewide campaign beginning November 25.

The initiative is part of the Women and Child Development Department's 'Orange the World' campaign, aimed at ending violence and gender discrimination against women and girls.

This year's campaign will focus on ensuring that survivors of violence can seek assistance without fear and on strengthening legal action against perpetrators.

Read more

Funding news

CortexSpark Ventures launches Rs 1,000 Cr deeptech fund

CortexSpark Ventures, a venture capital firm focused on deeptech and artificial intelligence segment, has launched a Rs 1,000 crore fund with an additional greenshoe option of Rs 400 crore.

CortexSpark Ventures, founded by former Infosys executives Vinay Peshwa and Sanjay Khanduri, will focus on startup investments across spacetech, defence tech, embodied AI and robotics, enterprise AI, medtech & Bio-AI, and energy and advanced materials.

Read more

Cosine Robots raises Rs 22.36 Cr to build made-in-India robot actuators

Bengaluru-based Cosine Robots has raised Rs 22.36 crore in a round led by deeptech fund Avaana Capital, with participation from WEH Ventures and angel investors. Founded by Kiran Mathew Koshy and Delip Thomas, the startup makes integrated servo actuators that combine motors, gearboxes, sensors, electronics and proprietary control software. Its joint-level controller runs a 25 kHz loop, or 25,000 updates per second. 

The company offers cycloidal and planetary actuators for industrial arms, cobots, quadrupeds and humanoids. The money will fund a new R&D and production facility covering machining, assembly, calibration and endurance testing, and expand the engineering team. Cosine aims to offer robot makers a cost-competitive alternative to established suppliers.

Other news

IIIT-Delhi to host eighth symposium on computational gastronomy

IIIT-Delhi's Complex Systems Laboratory will host GastroSym2026, the eighth edition of its symposium on computational gastronomy. The symposium brings together chefs, scientists, historians, entrepreneurs and policymakers. The field of computational gastronomy turns culinary knowledge into structured data that can be modelled and analysed. 

Speakers include chef Manjit Singh Gill, Prof. Ganesh Bagler, anthropologist Prof. Kurush F. Dalal, and Amura Health's Saravanan Balakrishnan. Sessions cover food safety, sensory science, fragrance, personalised nutrition, the gut microbiome and ageing. TasteTron will demonstrate a cooking-machine prototype; Foodoscope Technologies and Bettrlabs will also present. The event also features research posters and startup showcases.

Cashfree launches wallet that lets Indian users authorise AI agents to pay

Payments platform Cashfree has launched Cashfree Wallet, which it calls India's first wallet that lets users authorise personal AI agents to make payments for them. Users link the wallet to their agent with a mobile OTP, add money via UPI, card or net banking, and set budgets and spending rules. 

Agents pay only from the wallet balance; so they never see card, UPI or bank details. For now, Cashfree Wallet supports bill payments; travel, food, grocery and ecommerce are under testing. Developers can integrate through Cashfree's Agentpay MCP server; more than 100 agent and bot builders have already done so, said the company. Payment data is stored in India.

Resilience AI reaches nearly five million people and spaces, adds three advisors

Bengaluru-based Resilience AI, founded in November 2023, says its Resilience360 platform now covers nearly five million people and physical spaces across the US, UK, Canada and India, as it works towards futureproofing one billion by 2030. Co-founder Anshu Sharma and advisor Manu Gupta have left the company, while Sujata Saunik, Umit Bhatia and Firoz C joined as advisors in 2026.

More than 500 professionals in over 30 organisations hold Resilience360 certification. The platform is sold through four offerings: Basic, Forge, Spaces and Pro. The company aims to make physical climate risk assessment measurable and bankable across sectors, supported by its founders and advisory network.

GalaxEye picks Bellatrix Aerospace to power its next 30 Gen-II satellites

Bengaluru-based GalaxEye has awarded Bellatrix Aerospace a multi-year contract to supply Arka Hall-effect electric propulsion systems for its next 30 OptoSAR Gen-II satellites, announced at the India International Space Conclave 2026. Measured by satellite count, it is the largest business-to-business order between Indian private space companies since the sector opened in 2020.

The thrusters will place satellites in their slots, maintain spacing, avoid debris and handle end-of-life deorbiting. Bellatrix's thrusters were qualified in orbit on ISRO missions, and the company raised a $20 million pre-Series B in March 2026. GalaxEye's Mission Drishti launched in May 2026, but contact was lost after a geomagnetic storm.

QNu Labs and NIELIT sign MoU to build India's quantum-ready workforce

QNu Labs, a quantum cybersecurity company, has signed a memorandum of understanding with the National Institute of Electronics and Information Technology (NIELIT), a society under the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology, to strengthen quantum technology education and skills.

The two will develop training programmes in quantum technologies, including quantum-safe cybersecurity, and explore Quantum Labs at identified institutions through a hub-and-spoke model. Plans include industry-oriented curricula, hackathons, faculty development, train-the-trainer programmes, certification, internships and on-the-job training, wherever feasible and mutually agreed. The partnership aims to link industry expertise with institutional learning and prepare talent for India's evolving quantum landscape.

Vidyakul raises Rs 10 Cr in debt funding from Michael & Susan Dell Foundation

Vidyakul, a vernacular-first learning platform for state-board students, has secured Rs 10 crore in debt funding from the Michael & Susan Dell Foundation. The money will go towards expanding courses, assessments and personalised academic support for Classes 9 to 12, and towards its Hindi AI tools, which resolve about 1.2 million student questions a month.

It also plans pathways for students beyond Class 12. The company says 99.8% of its Bihar Class 12 students passed the 2026 board exams, against a statewide rate of 85%. More than 1.17 lakh students enrolled in its paid programmes in 2025-26, and its YouTube channels have over 15 million subscribers.

Pixxel signs MoUs with Centum Electronics and CS TECH Ai to advance space and geospatial technologies

Bengaluru-based Pixxel has signed two memoranda of understanding at the India International Space Conclave 2026. The agreement with Centum Electronics covers joint development of advanced electronics for satellite payloads and subsystems, drawing on Centum's decades of experience with ISRO missions.

The pact with CS TECH Ai (Ceinsys Tech) will explore geospatial data applications, orbital sustainability and enterprise dashboards that use satellite data and AI for infrastructure decision-making. Both follow an MoU with IIT Kanpur on hyperspectral research and AI-driven remote sensing. Pixxel raised $100 million in Series C funding earlier this year, taking its total capital to $195 million.

Flipkart Foundation's Sampark 2026 focuses on systemic change as Delhi outlines gig workers welfare board

The Flipkart Foundation hosted the fourth edition of its Sampark conference at Bharat Mandapam, New Delhi, themed on building institutions and local capabilities so that development outlasts individual programmes. The foundation says it has reached 41.5 lakh people across 17 states and union territories.

Delhi Cabinet Minister Kapil Mishra said the government is working towards a Gig Workers Welfare Board covering social security, healthcare and workplace safety, and urged skilling so delivery partners can move into store and warehouse roles. Panels and a keynote discussed community ownership, scaling through government partnerships and youth development, and the foundation recognised its NGO partners.

item.title: NVIDIA reinstates Jensen Huang as CEO
item.description: Just 11 days after his resignation from the company, Jensen Huang is back at Nvidia as president, CEO, and board director.
item.content:encoded:
Nvidia has reinstated co-founder Jensen Huang as its president, chief executive officer, and board director, with immediate effect, less than two weeks after his resignation from the company.

The unanimous decision follows discussions between Huang and the board, alongside inputs from senior US government officials, the company said.

“I am honored to return to NVIDIA and lead one of the most consequential technology companies in the world at the beginning of a new industrial revolution. I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment… I am grateful for the love and support of my family. I can’t wait to get back to work,” Huang said.

This marks a swift reversal of decisions at Nvidia, the world’s leading AI chipmaker. However, questions surrounding the circumstances of Huang's departure remain unresolved.

Huang’s resignation was announced on November 12. The board had subsequently cited "personal behaviour inconsistent with the company’s code of conduct and standards". The development came amid reports that Huang had been targeted in a foreign intelligence effort, following media coverage of his relationship with Alice Huang.

Nvidia had said it had no reason to believe that national security or company secrets had been compromised. However, it established an independent investigation into the matter.

Nvidia is also establishing a national security and export control oversight committee and recruiting a chief compliance officer, signalling that governance and regulatory scrutiny will remain its priorities.

Explaining the decision to reinstate Jensen Huang, board chair Harvey C. Jones said, “The board believes Jensen is the right person to lead NVIDIA, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers.”

Jones will remain as board chair.

The board also thanked CFO Colette Kress, who served as the interim chief executive, for her service.

Founded in 1993, Nvidia initially built its business around graphics processing units (GPUs), chips designed to handle many calculations simultaneously. Their parallel-processing capabilities have made them particularly valuable in the AI race, both for training models and running them in response to user requests. The company has consequently become a central player in the expansion of AI data centres.

Nvidia's financial performance underscores the stakes involves. The company reported a revenue of $115.8 billion for the third quarter of fiscal 2027, up 103% year on year, with data-centre revenue reaching $107.6 billion.

item.title: 94% of India's most-used online platforms still use dark patterns: LocalCircles
item.description: A LocalCircles study finds that 94% of India's 354 most-used online platforms continue to deploy dark patterns, with 37 of 45 sectors having no fully compliant platform.
item.content:encoded:
As many as 94% of India's most-used online platforms continue to use deceptive design practices, commonly known as dark patterns, despite growing regulatory scrutiny, according to a new study by LocalCircles.

The study analysed 354 online platforms across 45 sectors and found that only 20 were free of dark patterns. Further, 37 sectors had no platform that fully complied with the dark pattern guidelines.

The findings come weeks before the amended Consumer Protection (E-Commerce) Rules, 2026, take effect on January 1, 2027. Under the new rules, e-commerce companies must conduct annual self-audits and prominently display certificates declaring their platforms free of dark patterns.

Dark patterns or Dark UX are user interface designs that trick users into taking unintended actions such as buying a subscription, making payments or sharing personal data.

The study also found gaps in the self-declaration process. Of the 31 companies that had submitted a 'dark pattern free' declaration to the Central Consumer Protection Authority (CCPA), platforms operated by 23 companies, or 74%, were still found to have dark patterns. Only eight companies were found to be compliant.

Among publicly listed companies, 102 of the 108 consumer-facing online platforms analysed continued to have dark patterns. This means 94% of the platforms operated by listed companies still had deceptive design practices.

Online grocery, food delivery, OTT platforms show zero compliance

The study found that 37 of the 45 sectors analysed had no fully compliant platforms. These included online grocery, food delivery aggregators, taxi aggregators, OTT platforms, edtech, online banking, airlines, railway ticketing, mobile telecom services, online gaming, insurance and AI platforms.

B2B business marketplaces recorded the highest compliance at 100%, followed by car rental at 25%, e-commerce inventory platforms at 19%, e-commerce at 17% and quick commerce at 14%. Online payments recorded 11% compliance, while travel booking and digital lending reported 10% and 3%, respectively.

Forced action and drip pricing remain common

Forced action was the most prevalent dark pattern, appearing on 237 platforms, or 67% of those analysed. Drip pricing, where additional charges are introduced during the purchase process, was found on 222 platforms (63%).

Bait and switch practices were identified on 178 platforms (50%), while interface interference appeared on 170 platforms (48%). Other common practices included nagging (36%), subscription traps (32%) and privacy zuckering (23%).

The study also identified basket sneaking on 11% of platforms and false urgency on 10%.

The findings are based on complaints and experiences shared by more than 250,000 consumers across 392 districts, LocalCircles' AI-powered detection technology and public social media complaints.

Regulatory action against dark patterns has also increased. The CCPA penalised nine digital platforms in August 2026. Meanwhile, SEBI's Common Advertisement Code, notified in October, prohibits regulated entities from using dark patterns listed in the CCPA guidelines. The RBI has also issued directions barring banks and their sales agents from deploying such practices, effective January 1, 2027.

LocalCircles has urged the Department of Consumer Affairs and the CCPA to make dark-pattern compliance mandatory across all consumer-facing online platforms, in coordination with sectoral regulators. It has also called for publicly listed companies to display dark-pattern-free certificates.

item.title: CortexSpark Ventures launches Rs 1,000 Cr deeptech fund
item.description: CortexSpark Ventures will back deeptech startups that have created IP and looking to translate this into commercial applications
item.content:encoded:
CortexSpark Ventures, a venture capital firm focused on deeptech and artificial intelligence segment, has launched a Rs 1,000 crore fund with an additional greenshoe option of Rs 400 crore.

Founded by former Infosys executives Vinay Peshwa and Sanjay Khanduri, the company will focus on startup investments across spacetech, defence tech, embodied AI and robotics, enterprise AI, medtech & Bio-AI, and energy and advanced materials.

According to a statement, CortexSpark Ventures aims to back startups developing intellectual property and solving complex technological challenges. The firm's investment thesis focuses on startups with defensible intellectual property, strong technical foundations, experienced founders and clear pathways to commercialisation. It aims to bridge the gap between scientific innovation and commercial scale through capital, technical expertise and strategic support.

"India has built world-class technology services companies. The next opportunity is to create globally competitive technology product companies driven by original research and intellectual property,” said Vinay Peshwa, Managing Partner, CortexSpark Ventures.

The philosophy of this VC firm is, “The venture fund for AI, by AI,” as it aims to combine AI-enabled investment processes with scientific expertise, human judgement and global networks.

The fund's Investment Committee is chaired by Manoj Kohli, former country head of SoftBank Group and ex-CEO & MD of Bharti Airtel. The other advisors are N Vedachalam, former Director of ISRO's Liquid Propulsion Systems Centre and Ashutosh Sharma, former Secretary, Department of Science and Technology, Government of India.

"India has the scientific talent, engineering capabilities and entrepreneurial ambition to build globally competitive deep-tech companies. What is needed is an investment ecosystem that understands breakthrough technologies and supports their journey to commercial scale,” said Manoj Kohli, Chairman of the Investment Committee, CortexSpark Ventures.

According to this VC firm, deeptech startups often face longer development cycles, complex technical risks and higher capital requirements and it aims to address these challenges through scientific evaluation, commercial due diligence and active support for founders.

The firm is also developing CortexSpark OS, an AI-enabled fund management platform designed to support deal sourcing, screening, due diligence and portfolio monitoring.

item.title: IG Defence test-fires counter-drone micro-missile system
item.description: The company's indigenously developed micro-missile system JWALA MK-I was successfully tested at Pokhran, Rajasthan.
item.content:encoded:
IG Defence has successfully test-fired JWALA MK-I, an indigenously developed micro-missile system designed to counter unmanned aerial threats, at the Pokhran Test Range in Rajasthan.

The announcement was made by Bodhisattwa Sanghapriya, Founder and Chief Executive Officer of IG Defence. “India’s first indigenous Counter-UAS (CUAS) Micro-Missile System, JWALA MK-I, has been successfully test-fired by IG Defence at the Pokhran Test Range, Rajasthan,” he wrote in a LinkedIn post.

Highlighting the importance of developing domestic defence technologies, Sanghapriya said, “The future of warfare will be shaped by nations that innovate, develop and manufacture their own strategic technologies. India must not merely prepare for the future of warfare. India must build the technologies that will define it.” 

The development adds a missile-based approach to India’s expanding counter-drone capabilities, an increasingly important area of defence modernisation as the use of unmanned aircraft in military operations grows.

IG Defence describes JWALA as a short-range surface-to-air missile intended for use against unmanned aerial vehicles, with a claimed engagement range of 2-5 km. It represents a hard-kill approach, in which an incoming drone is physically destroyed. Soft-kill systems, by contrast, use techniques such as electronic jamming or signal spoofing to disrupt a drone’s control or navigation signals.

India already has several counter-drone programmes employing different technologies. Bharat Electronics Limited, in collaboration with the Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO), has developed the D4 Counter Drone System, which combines drone detection and tracking with soft- and hard-kill capabilities, according to the Department of Defence Production.

Private-sector participation is also growing in this space. Adani Defence and DRDO unveiled a vehicle-mounted counter-drone system at Aero India 2025, integrating radar, electronic jamming and a laser-based weapon.

In July 2026, Zen Technologies announced a man-portable anti-drone system designed for high-altitude operations, using radio-frequency detection and jamming.

item.title: Fintech startup Vegapay to raise Rs 38.4 Cr in Series A funding round led by Prosus
item.description: The round will also see participation from existing investors Elevation Capital, Vertex Ventures and Eximius Ventures.
item.content:encoded:
Vegapay, the Mumbai-headquartered digital lending and card management platform, will be raising Rs 38.4 crore in a Series A round of funding led by Prosus.

The regulatory filings of Vegapay reveal that this round will also see participation from existing investors, Elevation Capital, Vertex Ventures and Eximius Ventures.

Entrackr reported this development earlier.

A special resolution has been passed by Vegapay to issue 18,090 compulsory convertible preference shares (CCPS) at a price of Rs 21,221.92 per share, which leads to a total fundraise of Rs 38.4 crore.

Prosus will invest Rs 28.80 crore through its investment firm MIH Investments One BV. Elevation Capital will invest Rs 6.04 crore, and Vertex Ventures Rs 2.30 crore. Eximius will infuse Rs 1.25 crore.

Prior to this, Vegapay had raised Rs 37.9 crore in a pre-Series A round of funding led by Vertex Ventures. The round also saw participation from Elevation Capital and Eximius Ventures.

Founded by Gaurav Mittal, Himanshu Agrawal, Puneet Sharma, and Abhinav Garg in 2022, Vegapay is building a lending tech stack and a card management system that enables regulated entities and fintech firms to issue and increase penetration of card and lending in India.

The company offers a flexible pay-as-you-go model, reducing financial barriers. Flexibility, scalability, and speed are the platform's key differentiators, says Vegapay,

Prosus has become an active investor in the fintech segment of the Indian startup ecosystem. It has invested $100 million in Sachin Bansal-led Navi and $10 million in Bachatt.

Edited by Swetha Kannan

item.title: Log out after using WhatsApp Web to prevent account hijacking: MHA advises users
item.description: According to an advisory issued by the National Cybercrime Threat Analytics Unit of the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre, active WhatsApp Web sessions could be misused to access private messages, impersonate users, and carry out cyber fraud.
item.content:encoded:
The Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) has issued a cybersecurity advisory cautioning users about the potential misuse of authenticated WhatsApp Web sessions to gain access to their accounts.

The advisory, dated November 18, was issued by the National Cybercrime Threat Analytics Unit of the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C), under the MHA.

The advisory warned that leaving accounts logged in on office computers or shared devices could expose them to unauthorised access. This could allow malicious actors to read private messages, send messages while impersonating the account holder, access contacts and group conversations, and exploit trusted identities to carry out fraud, phishing and social-engineering attacks.

The advisory recommends that organisations avoid using WhatsApp Web on office computers, particularly in official and sensitive environments. Users have been advised against exchanging government, financial, confidential or other sensitive information through WhatsApp Web sessions on computers.

The I4C has cautioned that simply closing a browser window or tab should not be treated as logging out of WhatsApp Web. Users must manually terminate their sessions after completing their work and avoid leaving accounts permanently logged in.

If access is unavoidable, the agency recommends using 'incognito' or 'private browsing' mode on a trusted computer, followed by a manual logout. Users have also been advised against accessing WhatsApp Web through cyber cafes, public kiosks, hotel business centres, borrowed computers, or other untrusted systems.

The advisory further recommends keeping devices, operating systems, browsers and security software updated, avoiding suspicious downloads, and monitoring accounts for unexpected messages or unusual activity.

WhatsApp Web sessions targeted in 'Boss Scam'

The latest warning comes amid a rise in WhatsApp-linked account takeover fraud. In an August 7 advisory, the MHA warned corporates and finance professionals about a campaign known as the 'Boss Scam' or CEO impersonation fraud.

According to the ministry's statement published on the Press Information Bureau, fraudsters circulated malicious ZIP files disguised as account statements and regulatory communications, using names such as 'Statement of Account.zip', 'RBI.zip' and 'MCA.zip'.

The files contained malicious Windows executable (.exe) and Dynamic Link Library (.dll) files. Once extracted and executed on a Windows computer, the malware could compromise the device and hijack an active WhatsApp Web session.

Attackers subsequently used compromised accounts to circulate the same malicious files to contacts and groups. In more advanced cases, they impersonated senior executives and instructed finance employees to make urgent transfers to fraudulent bank accounts.

The MHA said it had alerted more than 58,000 potential victims through SMS messages sent under the header 'I4CMHA-G' in the preceding 30 days. More than 10,000 Indians had been protected through coordinated interventions, including the blocking of malicious infrastructure through the government's Sahyog Portal.

The ministry also said it had shared malware-related threat intelligence with the Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In), Microsoft Defender, and Indian cybersecurity companies, including Quick Heal, K7 Computing and Net Protector.

In its June 22 advisory, the I4C had first flagged the emerging 'Boss Scam' threat, warning that compromised WhatsApp accounts could be used to target employees with fraudulent financial instructions.

The MHA has advised users to regularly review the 'Linked Devices' section in WhatsApp and remove unfamiliar or inactive sessions. It has also urged companies to independently verify urgent payment instructions received through messaging platforms.

Edited by Swetha Kannan

item.title: Beyond tickets: How LightSprint.ai is building a multiplayer software factory where PMs and designers ship with engineers
item.description: AI made writing code faster. It did not make it easier for the people closest to customers to change the product. LightSprint.ai, part of NetApp Excellerator's Cohort 15, is changing that.
item.content:encoded:
It is Monday morning. A product manager has a customer escalation, a designer has spotted exactly where users drop off, and both know what should change. They write a ticket. It joins a backlog waiting on an engineering team that is already stretched. Weeks later, the change ships, often not quite as intended.

AI coding agents have made individual engineers dramatically faster, yet the way most companies build software has barely changed.

Enter LightSprint.ai, which is building a multiplayer software factory, one shared place where engineers, product managers and designers plan, build and ship together on the codebase they already have, with engineering approving every merge.

The problem: AI made coding single-player

Today's coding agents live in one developer's editor or terminal. One person drives, and everyone else falls out of sync. Planning stays buried in documents, context lives in someone's head, and reviewers approve large batches of AI-written code with little shared understanding of why it was written.

Prototyping tools showed non-engineers they could create software, but on a blank canvas. Real companies depend on complex codebases with years of conventions and review rules. A prototype can ignore all of that; a production change cannot, so the prototype gets rebuilt and the speed is lost.

The bottleneck has moved. Writing code is no longer the slowest step. Coordination is.

Why enterprises feel it most

For large organizations, every change needs to be traceable: which requirement it came from, which acceptance criteria it meets, and which tests prove it works. Teams must follow approved packages and design systems, and security teams want to know where code and

data live and who approved what. Opening AI coding to more people without that structure creates risk; withholding it leaves the backlog where it is.

LightSprint.ai's approach

LightSprint.ai sits on top of the coding agents teams already use and turns them into a shared workspace for the whole product team. It rests on three pillars.

  1. Spec first, with traceability built in. Anyone can describe a change in plain language. LightSprint.ai asks clarifying questions, drafts a spec with acceptance criteria, and the team agrees on the plan before any code is written, while it is still cheap to change. Each change stays traceable from requirement to spec to tests and the final pull request.
  2. Multiplayer by default. Product managers, designers and engineers work in the same live session. Anyone can join an agent, steer it, and review a live preview of the change. Shared skills and memory capture the team's conventions, so every teammate and agent builds the way the organization already works.
  3. Engineering in control. Engineers set up the environment once, and nobody else needs a local development setup. Agents work in isolated cloud sandboxes, credentials stay out of AI-written code, automated verification checks each change, and engineers approve every merge through the GitHub workflow they already use. Teams can bring their own models and LLM gateway.

The result is not fewer engineers. It is engineers spending their time on the decisions that need their judgment, while the people closest to customers ship the changes they understand best.

Building with NetApp

Through NetApp Excellerator, LightSprint.ai is working with NetApp teams on evaluating how a multiplayer software factory fits an enterprise environment: spec-driven development, traceability from requirement to test, adherence to approved packages and UI standards, and a security model that meets enterprise review.

"Coding agents made engineers faster, but most software teams are still single-player. The people closest to customers write tickets and wait," said Ben Ong, Co-founder and CEO of LightSprint.ai. "Working with NetApp through the Excellerator program has sharpened what enterprises need for a multiplayer model to work at scale: clear specs, end-to-end traceability and security built in from day one."

Early signs of a shift

Since starting with early users in April 2026, LightSprint.ai now works with over 100 companies, and non-engineers have shipped thousands of pull requests on the platform, with an aggregate merge rate averaging above 80%. Companies are adopting a "coding for all" strategy, where product, design and operations build alongside engineering.

And that Monday morning? The product manager and designer open a shared session, agree on the plan with an engineer, click through a live preview together, and the engineer approves the merge the same week. No ticket left waiting.

item.title: NVIDIA reinstates Jensen Huang as CEO; Sarvam unveils upgraded model amid Token Factory row
item.description: Nvidia has reinstated co-founder Jensen Huang as its president, CEO, and board director, less than two weeks after his resignation from the company. In other news, Sarvam’s new AI model promises better performance at a lower cost.
item.content:encoded:
Dear Reader,

In a quick turn of events, Nvidia has reinstated co-founder Jensen Huang as its president, CEO, and board director. 

This development comes less than two weeks after Huang’s resignation from the company. It follows discussions between Huang and the board, alongside inputs from senior US government officials, the company said.

In other news, Zoho’s Sridhar Vembu has said AI is transforming coding and intellectual work the way mechanisation impacted farming and weaving. 

Backing an observation by AI researcher Subbarao Kambhampati, Vembu said, in a post on X, “What happened to farmers and weavers and carpenters and ironsmiths in the waves of mechanization and automation is now starting to happen to mathematicians and programmers.”

Amid the backlash over hosting Chinese models on its Token Factory platform, Sarvam has clarified its AI strategy. 

Co-founder Pratyush Kumar said a model’s country of origin and the location of the infrastructure on which it runs are two different matters. He also emphasised that building inference infrastructure does not diminish Sarvam’s core focus on its own models. 

The company has released an upgraded model that it says delivers better performance at a lower cost. More on that below.

Meanwhile, the Ministry of Home Affairs has urged users to log out after using WhatsApp Web to prevent account hijacking. An advisory issued by the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre says active WhatsApp Web sessions could be misused to access private messages, impersonate users, and carry out cyber fraud. 

In today’s newsletter: 

  • Sarvam’s new AI model promises better performance at lower cost
  • Digital Naaris: A network of women micro-entrepreneurs 

Here’s your trivia for today: What does ‘dim sum’ mean in English? (Scroll down for the answer)

Artificial Intelligence

Sarvam’s new AI model promises better performance at lower cost

Sarvam AI has released Sarvam-105B-1711, a model designed for businesses handling large volumes of customer queries, phone calls, and software-based tasks. The company says the updated version of its 105B model follows instructions more reliably, uses digital tools better, and handles Indian languages more effectively, all at a lower cost. 

The latest release is part of a broader push by Sarvam to build models for different applications. It follows Sarvam Prism, a model designed to make quick, straightforward decisions; Bulbul V4 Flash, which turns written text into natural-sounding speech; and Saaras V4, which converts spoken language into text across 22 Indian languages.

More for less: 

  • Sarvam-105B-1711 was trained on Nvidia’s Blackwell B200 chips, powerful processors built for AI calculations. The model’s architecture activates only selected parts to generate each response, reducing computing requirements.
  • Potential uses include customer-service chatbots, AI voice assistants that speak with callers, and digital assistants that use software to complete tasks.
  • Sarvam is making the model’s learned settings, known as ‘weights’, available for download. Businesses with suitable computers can run the model themselves rather than relying entirely on Sarvam’s online service.

In-focus

How PayNearby is building a network of women micro-entrepreneurs 

PayNearby was founded in 2016 to enable neighbourhood stores to offer digital banking and financial services. As its reach expanded over the years, the company noticed that more men were accessing its services than women.

So, in 2024, the fintech platform launched Digital Naari to train women as financial and digital service providers serving other women in their communities. The company says the initiative now reaches women across more than 15,000 pin codes, helping them earn through transaction-based commissions.

Key takeaways:

  •  A Digital Naari is a banking touchpoint within a community, operated by a woman agent. After training, agents use a mobile phone to provide services such as banking, insurance, credit, bill payments and telehealth.
  • PayNearby says about 80% of the women joining the programme are first-time entrepreneurs. Participants include women from low-income households, single mothers and widows supporting their families. 
  • Digital Naari not only creates an income opportunity for women, it also makes financial services more accessible to other women within their communities.

item.title: Ionic Wealth secures Rs 177 Cr from Angel One, others
item.description: The wealthtech platform will use the funds to expand its portfolio of services, technology, and footprint in India and beyond.
item.content:encoded:
Ionic Wealth, a wealthtech platform and a subsidiary of Angel One, has raised Rs 177 crore in strategic funding to accelerate its growth trajectory. The funding was led by Angel One and marquee families.

This takes the company's cumulative funding to Rs 466 crore. According to a statement, all investors from the previous round also participated in the latest round, comprising business families, Bollywood personalities, fintech entrepreneurs, global CXOs, board advisors and media houses.

As part of its growth plans, Ionic Wealth will strengthen portfolio-led proposition, global capabilities, and AI integration in the wealth-tech experience. It will also scale the UHNI business and expand its footprint in India and beyond.

The fresh capital will be used to double down on the company's early bets, leverage technology, advance GIFT City-led global investing, and develop a differentiated UHNI proposition for India's leading families.

Ionic Wealth was founded in 2024 by Srikanth Subramanian, Shobhit Mathur, and Dharmendra Jain. It today has an AUM (assets under management) of over Rs 16,000 crore and more than 2,900 HNI and UHNI clients across 12+ cities.

“As investor needs evolve, our focus is to move beyond traditional product-led offerings towards a more comprehensive platform approach to wealth creation, informed by our institutional-grade investment intelligence across global markets and asset classes,” said Srikanth Subramanian, Co-founder and CEO, Ionic Wealth.

Ionic Wealth attributes its growth to rising HNI numbers, appreciation in asset value, and growing income and savings.

Dinesh Thakkar, Founder, Chairman and Managing Director, Angel One, said, “India’s wealth management industry is at an important inflection point, driven by the growing aspirations of affluent investors and the increasing sophistication of their financial needs.

"Ionic is being built to serve this opportunity by bringing together investment expertise, technology and a client-first approach. We have strong conviction in the founding team and the institution they are building."
